worldSentence: Washington is trying to stabilize its relationship with China while the Iran war hardens, bond yields rise and new evidence shows that the same AI race now reaches diplomacy, biology, shopping and national security.
standfirst: Xi Jinping arrived in Washington for a state visit expected to extend the U.S.–China trade truce without resolving technology, Taiwan or Iran. Iran’s president answered tentative diplomacy with a defiant U.N. speech, while hot U.S. activity data and a weak Treasury auction pushed rate expectations higher. Qatar announced two different attempts to turn partnerships into local operating capability. Anthropic reported an AI-assisted biological discovery, technology leaders asked the U.N. for guardrails, and an alleged FBI data breach exposed the human cost of compromised identity systems. Consumer research suggests AI is already influencing food choices; America’s air-traffic failures show why infrastructure modernization must be judged as a system, not a shopping list.

connected.title: The useful test today is whether a system works beyond the announcement.

signals.label: TRADE TRUCE
signals.text: Expected from the Trump–Xi visit; the unresolved restrictions and enforcement matter more.

signals.label: QATAR HUBS
signals.text: Manufacturing and venture platforms proposed; facilities, staffing and mandates are not yet operating.

signals.label: AI BIOLOGY
signals.text: Anthropic reports a novel enzyme system; independent experimental validation is the next gate.

connected.note: A summit is not strategic alignment, a memorandum is not an operating hub, a model-generated hypothesis is not a replicated discovery, and a backup line is not resilience if it shares the same failure domain. Across diplomacy, technology and infrastructure, implementation is the story after the headline.

stories.title: Xi arrived in Washington for a state visit built to extend stability, not settle the rivalry.
stories.changed: President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday for his first U.S. visit in more than a decade. The White House signaled that the current trade truce would be extended. Both governments want to prevent another tariff spiral, but the summit agenda still includes technology controls, Taiwan, Iran and competing approaches to AI governance.
stories.matters: An extension can reduce immediate commercial uncertainty without resolving the structure of the conflict. Firms can plan around tariffs only if the rules and duration are clear; semiconductor, AI and investment restrictions can keep tightening even while headline trade tensions cool. The visit is therefore a test of managed rivalry rather than a path to a grand bargain.
stories.watch: The length and legal terms of the trade-truce extension; any tariff or purchase commitments; export-control language; Taiwan and Iran statements; whether the leaders create working-level mechanisms; and which claims appear in a joint text rather than separate briefings.

group.label: The lead
group.title: The world’s largest economies are buying time, not resolving their contest.
group.note: The state visit lowers the temperature while the hardest issues remain open.

background.title: Stability is an outcome, but it is not settlement
background.text: The two governments stepped back from last year’s tariff escalation and met in Beijing in May. This visit extends that effort while each side continues to build leverage: China through trade scale and industrial capacity, the United States through market access, advanced-chip controls and alliance networks. A truce can be economically valuable because it narrows the range of near-term disruption. It does not erase the incentives driving technology restrictions, Taiwan deterrence or competition for influence in the Gulf.
background.known: Xi arrived, the leaders are meeting, and both sides have signaled an extension of the trade truce.
background.new: The relationship has moved from preparatory talks to a formal state visit with a concrete near-term deliverable.

left.label: Visible progress
left.text: The visit itself and expected truce extension show both capitals still value guardrails.

right.label: Unresolved substance
right.text: No durable agreement on export controls, Taiwan, AI or Iran has been announced.

sources.label: AP · Xi arrives and the trade truce is expected to be extended
Reuters · issues facing the Trump–Xi summit

stories.title: Iran’s president answered the first reported contact with defiance, exposing how far talks remain from terms.
stories.changed: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian used a rare wartime address to the U.N. General Assembly to call Iranians victims of U.S. terrorism and say the country would fight until its last breath. His speech came one day after Donald Trump said U.S. envoys held a three-hour meeting with Iranian mediators and after Trump threatened massive escalation if no deal is reached.
stories.matters: The speech does not prove private diplomacy has failed, but it sharply limits the case for treating contact as de-escalation. Leaders often negotiate while using uncompromising public language; the danger is that military operations, domestic politics and prestige narrow the room for sequencing concessions. Energy and shipping risks remain attached to what the parties do, not the existence of a channel.
stories.watch: Whether Iran confirms the reported meeting; continued intermediary contacts; attacks on Gulf infrastructure and shipping; a written ceasefire sequence; Hormuz access; sanctions and verification terms; and whether public rhetoric changes after the Trump–Xi meeting.

group.label: The world beyond the lead
group.title: The diplomatic channel exists inside an openly hardening war.
group.note: Pezeshkian’s U.N. speech widened the gap between contact and settlement.

background.title: Public defiance and private bargaining can coexist
background.text: Governments at war speak to several audiences at once: the adversary, citizens, military institutions, allies and potential mediators. Defiant language can protect negotiating room by denying the appearance of capitulation, but it also raises the political cost of compromise. The practical test is whether representatives exchange a sequence for stopping attacks, reopening Hormuz and verifying commitments. None of those terms is public.
background.known: Pezeshkian delivered the speech; Trump reported the earlier meeting; the war and shipping disruption continue.
background.new: Iran’s president has now supplied Tehran’s most visible public response to the claimed diplomatic opening.

left.label: Confirmed posture
left.text: The Iranian president publicly rejected surrender and blamed the United States.

right.label: Private process unclear
right.text: Iran has not publicly detailed the reported talks or any negotiating text.

sources.label: AP · Pezeshkian’s wartime U.N. address
AP · Trump’s U.N. speech and reported U.S.–Iran contact

stories.title: A hot U.S. activity reading and weak Treasury auction pushed the higher-rate regime deeper into markets.
stories.changed: U.S. business activity accelerated to its strongest pace in more than five years in September, while price pressures persisted. A poorly received five-year Treasury auction added to bond selling and pushed the five-year yield above 5% for the first time since 2007. The dollar index held near a two-month high around 101.1, and traders assigned roughly a 70% probability to another Federal Reserve increase in October.
stories.matters: The repricing is no longer only an energy-war story. Strong demand, price pressure and weaker appetite for government debt can all lift borrowing costs. That affects valuations, refinancing and currencies even if oil later falls. It also widens the gap between a hoped-for diplomatic relief rally and the domestic data the Fed actually uses.
stories.watch: Weekly jobless claims; incoming inflation data; Fed speakers; the October meeting; demand at upcoming Treasury auctions; five- and ten-year yields; the yen and intervention risk; and whether activity data weaken before pricing assumes a full tightening cycle.

group.label: Economy & markets
group.title: Rates are being driven by demand and bond supply as well as oil.
group.note: The five-year yield crossing 5% makes the repricing tangible.

background.title: Why a weak auction matters
background.text: Central banks set short-term policy rates, but market yields also reflect inflation expectations, government borrowing and the return investors demand to hold duration. When an auction clears weakly, yields rise until buyers accept the price. That can tighten financial conditions without a new Fed decision. Strong business activity reinforces the move because it suggests demand can tolerate—and may require—more restraint.
background.known: The activity survey strengthened, the auction was weak, yields rose and the dollar remained firm.
background.new: Market pricing now gives another October rate increase a substantially higher probability than one week ago.

left.label: Observed market move
left.text: Five-year yields crossed 5% and the dollar held near a two-month high.

right.label: Forecast, not policy
right.text: Futures probabilities can reverse; the Fed has not precommitted to an October increase.

sources.label: Reuters · dollar, PMI, auction and rate expectations
Reuters · bonds, oil and the day’s policy watchpoints

stories.title: Qatar announced two hub strategies: industrial servicing with Honeywell and venture scaling with LG NOVA.
stories.changed: Qatar Free Zones Authority and Honeywell Technologies signed an MoU to explore a manufacturing and service hub for Sundyne pumps used in energy and process industries. Separately, Invest Qatar, Aurion Capital and LG NOVA agreed to explore investment and venture-building programs, including a proposed Qatar Science and Technology Park hub for LG NOVA-affiliated companies across AI, digital health, fintech, infrastructure, sports and media.
stories.matters: The announcements represent two different diversification mechanisms. The Honeywell proposal localizes maintenance and machining around an installed industrial base. The LG NOVA proposal tries to import a pipeline of technology ventures and help them scale regionally. Both could create capability, but only if the local work, customers, talent and capital mandates are real.
stories.watch: Final investment decisions; facility location and commissioning dates; headcount and training commitments; licensed activities; supplier development; the number of ventures placed in Qatar; capital actually deployed; customers won; and how much work is performed locally rather than coordinated from Doha.

group.label: Qatar & the Gulf
group.title: Diversification is being pursued through two distinct operating models.
group.note: One serves physical industry; the other tries to build a technology-company pipeline.

background.title: The difference between a service hub and an innovation hub
background.text: Industrial-service localization starts with known equipment, recurring maintenance demand and regional customers. Venture platforms start with uncertain companies and need capital, product-market fit and market access. The first can deepen supply chains; the second can create new ones. Measuring them with the same announcement count would hide their economics. Each needs a specific operating scorecard.
background.known: The MoUs were signed and their intended sectors and locations were publicly described.
background.new: The proposals add concrete hub concepts to Qatar’s broader diversification and investment-promotion strategy.

left.label: Defined mechanisms
left.text: Sundyne servicing and an LG NOVA venture platform identify actual operating functions.

right.label: Execution still pending
right.text: No final investment, commissioned facility, staffing level or venture cohort has been disclosed.

sources.label: QNA · QFZ and Honeywell propose manufacturing and service hub
QNA · Invest Qatar, Aurion Capital and LG NOVA venture platform

stories.title: Anthropic says Claude identified a previously unrecognized enzyme system in genomic data.
stories.changed: Anthropic reported that Claude analyzed large DNA databases and identified what the company calls array-associated reverse transcriptases, or ART: a broader system involving a known reverse transcriptase, repeating non-coding DNA and another protein. The company describes it as the first result from its expanding biology-research effort and says the architecture has features reminiscent of CRISPR systems.
stories.matters: This is a more informative AI-science claim than a benchmark because it proposes a testable biological object. If independently confirmed, it would show a model contributing to hypothesis generation across large sequence databases. The value is not that AI replaces experimental biology; it is that computation may surface patterns worth spending scarce laboratory time on.
stories.watch: A preprint or peer-reviewed paper; methods and training-data disclosure; independent teams reproducing the pattern; wet-lab confirmation of the system’s function; false-positive rates; whether the finding leads to a usable tool; and how Anthropic separates model contribution from human interpretation.

group.label: AI & technology
group.title: AI’s most consequential claims are moving from chat into testable science.
group.note: The discovery is specific enough to verify—and still needs verification.

background.title: Discovery has several gates
background.text: Finding a statistical pattern in sequence data is not the same as showing what the system does in a cell. A credible chain moves from computational identification to a documented method, independent replication, experimental validation and eventually a useful mechanism. Claude may have contributed at the first stage. The scientific significance depends on the later ones.
background.known: Anthropic publicly described the system and Claude’s role in recognizing its broader architecture.
background.new: The claim gives Anthropic’s biology program its first named, falsifiable research result.

left.label: Testable claim
left.text: The proposed system has named components that other researchers can search for and examine.

right.label: Validation gap
right.text: Functional significance, reproducibility and practical use have not yet been independently demonstrated.

sources.label: Reuters · Anthropic reports the AI-assisted enzyme-system finding

stories.title: AI leaders asked the U.N. for control mechanisms, while governments still disagree over who should write them.
stories.changed: Executives from major AI firms addressed the U.N. Security Council and urged international action on risks created by rapidly advancing systems. The appeal arrived as the United States rejected a broad global regulatory scheme and argued that slowing development could advantage China. The event made the governance contradiction explicit: builders are asking states for guardrails while states compete through the same technology.
stories.matters: International declarations matter only if they become measurable duties: incident reporting, model evaluations, access controls, compute transparency or liability. Competition makes agreement harder because every restraint is judged against another country’s capacity. Voluntary concern without common definitions can produce reassurance while deployment continues unchanged.
stories.watch: A draft instrument rather than speeches; participating governments; thresholds defining covered systems; mandatory reporting and independent evaluation; treatment of open models; enforcement; and whether U.S. and Chinese officials accept any reciprocal transparency.

group.label: Technology governance
group.title: The risk consensus is advancing faster than the rulebook.
group.note: The next meaningful development is enforceable text, not another warning.

background.title: Why the U.N. venue changes the question
background.text: Domestic AI rules can govern firms inside one jurisdiction. Frontier systems, chips, cloud infrastructure and model access cross borders, so national rules leave gaps. The Security Council adds geopolitical weight but also veto politics. Any workable regime must define what is being controlled, how compliance is observed and why rivals should believe each other.
background.known: Technology leaders publicly requested stronger international control and governments articulated different approaches.
background.new: The governance debate has moved into the Security Council at the same moment AI is central to U.S.–China competition.

left.label: Shared concern
left.text: Industry leaders and multiple governments accept that advanced AI can create cross-border risks.

right.label: No common regime
right.text: There is no agreed threshold, inspection mechanism or enforcement system.

sources.label: AP · technology leaders appeal to the U.N. over AI risk
Reuters · AI governance among the Trump–Xi summit issues

stories.title: The FBI is investigating a claim that its jobs portal exposed agents, applicants and families.
stories.changed: The FBI said it is investigating the ShinyHunters group’s claim that it compromised FBIJobs.gov and obtained sensitive personally identifiable information on thousands of employees and applicants. The group claimed to hold data on agents and people who applied for jobs. The scope and authenticity of the stolen material have not been independently established.
stories.matters: A recruitment system can become a national-security system because applicants disclose identity, history and relationships. Even routine personal data can enable extortion, impersonation, doxxing or harassment when attached to law-enforcement personnel. The story is therefore about data classification and architecture, not only perimeter defense.
stories.watch: FBI confirmation of affected systems and records; notifications to individuals; evidence posted by the attackers; whether employee and applicant databases were segmented; persistence inside the network; identity-protection measures; and any operational impact on agents or investigations.

group.label: Cybersecurity
group.title: Administrative systems can carry operational risk.
group.note: The breach claim is serious; its exact scope remains unverified.

background.title: Data sensitivity depends on who the subject is
background.text: Names, addresses, employment histories and family links may look like standard human-resources data. For law-enforcement personnel, the same fields can reveal assignments, expose relatives and support targeted coercion. Security design therefore needs to classify data by consequence, limit collection, segment systems and monitor access—not simply label a jobs website as low risk.
background.known: The FBI acknowledged the claim and opened an investigation into the portal and alleged personal-data impact.
background.new: A named group has asserted access to both the recruitment surface and sensitive identity records.

left.label: Confirmed response
left.text: The FBI says it is aware of and investigating the claimed compromise.

right.label: Claim not yet verified
right.text: The number of records, their authenticity and the attackers’ access path remain unknown.

sources.label: AP · FBI investigates jobs-site and employee-data claim

stories.title: Conagra says AI-guided food discovery is reinforcing protein, health-goal and bold-flavor demand.
stories.changed: Conagra Brands said Americans are increasingly asking AI systems what to eat and snack on. Its work with Circana analyzed more than 53 million shopping transactions across 17,000 products in the $198.2 billion U.S. snacking market. The company links AI-assisted discovery with demand for high-protein foods, bold flavors and products aligned to specific health goals, alongside the effects of weight-loss drugs and health policy.
stories.matters: Recommendation interfaces can change which product attributes consumers search for before they reach a shelf or delivery app. For food operators, that raises the value of clear ingredients, protein, portioning and machine-readable product data. But Conagra’s evidence shows association and commercial interpretation, not that AI caused every purchasing shift.
stories.watch: Independent research on AI-assisted food discovery; conversion from queries to purchases; changes in search and retailer rankings; product reformulation; portion sizes; repeat purchase; whether high-protein demand persists; and how brands make claims legible without drifting into unsupported health marketing.

group.label: Consumer & retail
group.title: AI is beginning to sit upstream of the shopping journey.
group.note: The emerging advantage may be discoverability as much as advertising.

background.title: From search terms to product architecture
background.text: Traditional food discovery happened through shelves, menus, advertising and search engines. Conversational systems let consumers begin with a goal—more protein, lower calories, a particular flavor—and receive a compressed set of suggestions. That can reward products whose attributes are explicit and well structured. It can also amplify errors or marketing claims if recommendation systems lack reliable data.
background.known: Conagra and Circana analyzed a large transaction dataset and reported strong shifts in stated preferences and category growth.
background.new: A major food company is now treating AI-mediated discovery as an input to product and demand strategy.

left.label: Commercial signal
left.text: The analysis covers 53 million transactions and 17,000 products.

right.label: Causality uncertain
right.text: Weight-loss drugs, health policy, demographics and prices are changing demand at the same time.

sources.label: Reuters · Conagra on AI and changing U.S. snack choices

stories.title: The Northeast outage exposed a modernization problem larger than one severed cable.
stories.changed: Reuters documented an air-traffic system still dependent on decades-old telecommunications, incompatible platforms, old Compaq computers and replacement parts sourced through secondary markets. Monday’s Northeast disruption combined a failed circuit at the Philadelphia facility with a separately severed backup fiber, delaying or canceling thousands of flights. Officials say the fragility will persist without a much larger overhaul.
stories.matters: The new information turns a single outage into an architecture problem. Modernization programs can spend billions while preserving hidden dependencies, legacy interfaces and incomplete failover. Aviation networks amplify local failures because aircraft, crews, gates and passenger connections move out of sequence faster than they can be restored.
stories.watch: The FAA root-cause report; a funded architecture and delivery schedule; retirement dates for legacy systems; independent routing of backup circuits; staffing and integration tests; procurement accountability; and operational metrics showing that failover works under load rather than only in demonstrations.

group.label: Aviation
group.title: Resilience depends on architecture, not the age of individual boxes.
group.note: A system-wide overhaul must remove common failure paths while operations continue.

background.title: Why replacing equipment is not enough
background.text: Air-traffic control is a live, safety-critical network. New components must interoperate with old ones during a long transition, which can create more interfaces before it creates simplicity. A successful overhaul needs service continuity, independent communications routes, tested failover, data migration and clear responsibility across vendors and facilities. The hardest work is changing the system without stopping it.
background.known: The latest outage involved separate primary and backup failures; Reuters identified extensive legacy dependencies across the wider network.
background.new: The incident now has a broader inventory of systemic vulnerabilities rather than a single-cable explanation.

left.label: Visible fragility
left.text: One circuit failure and one construction cut disrupted a major multi-airport region.

right.label: Delivery risk
right.text: Funding and procurement do not guarantee compatible systems or proven failover.

sources.label: Reuters · legacy technology and stalled U.S. air-traffic upgrades
AP · the Philadelphia communications failure and backup cut

radar.label: Qatar finance
radar.title: QFC signed new cooperation memoranda in Beijing and Hong Kong.
radar.text: The direction fits Qatar’s effort to connect Asian capital and digital infrastructure. Watch licensed activity, investment flows and firms actually established through the relationships.

radar.label: Oil products
radar.title: Diesel refining margins reached a record even while crude sat near two-week lows.
radar.text: A possible U.S. diesel-export restriction and disrupted Middle East supply are separating product scarcity from crude availability. Watch policy, jet-fuel spreads and physical cargo flows.

radar.label: Weather risk
radar.title: Two Pacific hurricanes are creating simultaneous landslide and island risks.
radar.text: Polo threatens southwest Mexico while Nolo approaches Hawaii. Watch official evacuation orders, rainfall and infrastructure impacts rather than category headlines alone.

attention.title: The Trump–Xi summit issue map
attention.text: Read the Reuters factbox for the cleanest separation of trade, Taiwan, Iran and AI—issues that can move independently even during one state visit.

ignore.title: A trade-truce extension described as a strategic reset
ignore.text: Reducing immediate tariff risk is valuable. It does not resolve export controls, Taiwan, AI competition or enforcement, and should not be read as alignment.

history.title: The shipping container changed the world only after competitors agreed on the box.
history.deck: In 1956, the converted tanker Ideal-X carried 58 trailer bodies from New Jersey to Texas. The voyage is often treated as the invention of containerization. The harder achievement came afterward: turning one company’s equipment into a shared intermodal system. Ports, railways, truckers, governments and rivals had to accept common dimensions, corner fittings, strength tests and identification rules. Standardization made the box transferable—and made global supply chains possible.
history.thesis: The container’s power came less from its steel walls than from an institutional agreement that let thousands of independent machines and organizations handle the same object without renegotiating every transfer.

sections.title: Before the box, the port handled pieces
sections.text: Most general cargo arrived as break-bulk: sacks, crates, barrels and odd-shaped machinery that longshore workers moved between warehouses, nets, slings, trucks and ship holds. Ships could spend days in port while cargo was counted, sorted and stowed. Damage and theft were difficult to prevent because goods changed hands repeatedly. Containers were not a completely new idea; railways and militaries had used boxes before. What was missing was a commercial system that connected the ship to the inland journey and made mechanical transfer cheaper than handling each piece.

sections.title: McLean redesigned the journey, not merely the vessel
sections.text: Malcom McLean built a large trucking business and understood that the expensive delay was the transfer between modes. After acquiring a steamship company, he adapted the Ideal-X to carry detachable trailer bodies. On 26 April 1956, it sailed from Newark to Houston with 58 containers on deck. The important unit was now a sealed load that could travel from customer to truck, ship and destination with far less handling. Sea-Land, the company that emerged from the experiment, also developed chassis, cranes and ships around that flow.

sections.title: Early success produced a compatibility problem
sections.text: McLean’s containers were not the only design. Sea-Land used 35-foot boxes; Matson developed 24-foot units suited to heavy Hawaiian cargo; other operators favored different lengths for regional roads and loads. Each proprietary geometry demanded its own cranes, ship cells, trailers and storage patterns. A port choosing one system risked excluding another. The industry could gain efficiency inside individual networks while losing it between them. Without compatibility, containerization remained a collection of private islands rather than a global network.

sections.title: Standards converted private inventions into public infrastructure
sections.text: The International Organization for Standardization created its freight-container committee in 1961. Governments, carriers and manufacturers negotiated classifications, dimensions, strength ratings, handling points and markings. McLean’s relevant patents were made available to ISO without charge. In 1968, ISO published its first freight-container standard. The familiar twenty- and forty-foot families and standardized corner fittings let equipment built by different firms connect. A crane did not need to know whose box it lifted; it needed to know where the corners were and what loads the structure could bear.

sections.title: Ports had to be rebuilt around flow
sections.text: A standardized box still required immense fixed investment. Ports needed deep berths, high-capacity cranes, paved yards, rail links and large areas for stacking and truck access. Oakland had land and connections and embraced the system; San Francisco’s constrained waterfront lost its leading position. Containerization therefore did not simply make existing ports more efficient. It redistributed trade toward places able to redesign themselves around the new interface. The same logic later produced enormous hub ports and inland logistics parks.

sections.title: Labor productivity rose while waterfront work contracted
sections.text: Mechanization removed repeated lifting, sorting and tallying. Ships spent less time idle, cargo losses fell and each worker could move far more freight. Those gains also reduced demand for traditional longshore labor and shifted work toward crane operation, trucking, maintenance and logistics. Adoption required political bargaining as well as engineering. The container is a reminder that productivity improvements create concentrated disruption even when the wider economy gains from cheaper, faster transport.

sections.title: War accelerated a commercial network
sections.text: The U.S. military’s logistics crisis in Vietnam gave Sea-Land a large, demanding customer. Beginning in the mid-1960s, container services moved supplies across the Pacific and demonstrated the value of sealed loads, scheduled ships and faster transfer at scale. Military demand helped expand ships, terminals and routes that also served commerce. The system’s advantage became cumulative: every compatible crane, chassis, port and route made the standard more useful, encouraging the next investment.

sections.title: The box enabled globalization—and made its dependencies visible
sections.text: Standard containers reduced transport friction enough for firms to split production across countries, hold less inventory and serve distant markets. They expanded consumer choice and helped remote producers reach global buyers. The same concentration created new vulnerabilities. A blocked canal, closed terminal, missing chassis or shortage of empty boxes can propagate through the network because so many supply chains share the interface. Standardization does not eliminate risk; it makes coordination cheaper while increasing the value—and consequence—of the common system.

sections.title: The deepest innovation was agreement
sections.text: A steel box is easy to imitate. A global protocol across ships, ports, railways, roads, insurers, customs agencies and competitors is not. Containerization worked because dimensions, corner fittings, tests and identifiers became dependable enough that participants could invest without controlling the whole chain. That pattern appears in payment rails, internet protocols and aviation standards: networks scale when rivals can connect through a stable interface. The mundane specification is often where the real revolution lives.

timeline.text: General cargo is mostly loaded and unloaded piece by piece as break-bulk.
Ideal-X sails from Newark to Houston carrying 58 detachable trailer bodies.
Sea-Land expands container service beyond the continental United States.
ISO creates Technical Committee 104 for freight-container standards.
U.S. military logistics in Vietnam accelerates large-scale container use.
ISO publishes its first international freight-container standard.
Standardized intermodal containers reshape major ports and trade routes.
Dimensions, corner fittings, tests and identification codes remain shared infrastructure for global freight.
